quizzes.title: Electron Configuration
quizzes.description: 30 questions on neutral atoms in the ground state. Brackets represent a noble-gas core; superscripts show electrons in each subshell.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral hydrogen atom (H)?
questions.explanation: A neutral hydrogen atom has 1 electron. Its ground-state electron configuration is 1s¹.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral helium atom (He)?
questions.explanation: A neutral helium atom has 2 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is 1s².

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral lithium atom (Li)?
questions.explanation: A neutral lithium atom has 3 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [He] 2s¹.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral beryllium atom (Be)?
questions.explanation: A neutral beryllium atom has 4 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [He] 2s².

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral boron atom (B)?
questions.explanation: A neutral boron atom has 5 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [He] 2s² 2p¹.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral carbon atom (C)?
questions.explanation: A neutral carbon atom has 6 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [He] 2s² 2p².

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral nitrogen atom (N)?
questions.explanation: A neutral nitrogen atom has 7 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [He] 2s² 2p³.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral oxygen atom (O)?
questions.explanation: A neutral oxygen atom has 8 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [He] 2s² 2p⁴.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral fluorine atom (F)?
questions.explanation: A neutral fluorine atom has 9 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [He] 2s² 2p⁵.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral neon atom (Ne)?
questions.explanation: A neutral neon atom has 10 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [He] 2s² 2p⁶.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral sodium atom (Na)?
questions.explanation: A neutral sodium atom has 11 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ne] 3s¹.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral magnesium atom (Mg)?
questions.explanation: A neutral magnesium atom has 12 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ne] 3s².

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral aluminum atom (Al)?
questions.explanation: A neutral aluminum atom has 13 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ne] 3s² 3p¹.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral silicon atom (Si)?
questions.explanation: A neutral silicon atom has 14 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ne] 3s² 3p².

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral phosphorus atom (P)?
questions.explanation: A neutral phosphorus atom has 15 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ne] 3s² 3p³.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral sulfur atom (S)?
questions.explanation: A neutral sulfur atom has 16 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral chlorine atom (Cl)?
questions.explanation: A neutral chlorine atom has 17 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁵.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral argon atom (Ar)?
questions.explanation: A neutral argon atom has 18 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral potassium atom (K)?
questions.explanation: A neutral potassium atom has 19 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ar] 4s¹.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral calcium atom (Ca)?
questions.explanation: A neutral calcium atom has 20 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ar] 4s².

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral scandium atom (Sc)?
questions.explanation: A neutral scandium atom has 21 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ar] 3d¹ 4s².

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral titanium atom (Ti)?
questions.explanation: A neutral titanium atom has 22 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ar] 3d² 4s².

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral vanadium atom (V)?
questions.explanation: A neutral vanadium atom has 23 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ar] 3d³ 4s².

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral chromium atom (Cr)?
questions.explanation: A neutral chromium atom has 24 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹. This is an exception to the simple filling-order prediction.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral manganese atom (Mn)?
questions.explanation: A neutral manganese atom has 25 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s².

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral iron atom (Fe)?
questions.explanation: A neutral iron atom has 26 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s².

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral cobalt atom (Co)?
questions.explanation: A neutral cobalt atom has 27 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s².

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral nickel atom (Ni)?
questions.explanation: A neutral nickel atom has 28 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s².

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral copper atom (Cu)?
questions.explanation: A neutral copper atom has 29 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. This is an exception to the simple filling-order prediction.

questions.prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral zinc atom (Zn)?
questions.explanation: A neutral zinc atom has 30 electrons. Its ground-state electron configuration is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s².

H.name: Hydrogen
H.fact: It is the lightest element and the most abundant element in the universe.
H.uses: Used to manufacture ammonia for fertilizers and as a reactant in fuel cells.

He.name: Helium
He.fact: Its boiling point is lower than that of any other element.
He.uses: Liquid helium cools superconducting magnets, including those in MRI scanners.

Li.name: Lithium
Li.uses: Lithium compounds are used in rechargeable lithium-ion batteries.

Be.name: Beryllium
Be.fact: It combines low density with high stiffness.
Be.uses: Used in specialized aerospace components and X-ray windows.

B.name: Boron
B.fact: Boron is a metalloid, with properties between those of metals and nonmetals.
B.uses: Boron compounds are used in heat-resistant borosilicate glass.

C.name: Carbon
C.fact: Diamond and graphite are different structural forms of carbon.
C.uses: Graphite is used in pencil cores and battery electrodes; diamond is used in cutting tools.

N.name: Nitrogen
N.fact: Nitrogen gas makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere.
N.uses: Used to manufacture ammonia; liquid nitrogen provides very low-temperature cooling.

O.name: Oxygen
O.fact: Oxygen supports combustion but is not itself a fuel.
O.uses: Used in steelmaking and medical oxygen supplies.

F.name: Fluorine
F.fact: It is the most electronegative element.
F.uses: Fluoride compounds are used in toothpaste; fluorine-containing polymers include PTFE.

Ne.name: Neon
Ne.fact: Electrically excited neon gas emits a reddish-orange light.
Ne.uses: Used in illuminated signs and indicator lamps.

Na.name: Sodium
Na.fact: Its symbol comes from the Latin name natrium.
Na.uses: Sodium compounds are used in table salt, glass production, and many industrial processes.

Mg.name: Magnesium
Mg.fact: Magnesium burns with an intense white light.
Mg.uses: Used in lightweight alloys and in flares and fireworks.

Al.name: Aluminum
Al.fact: A thin oxide layer helps protect the metal from further corrosion.
Al.uses: Used in aircraft, beverage cans, foil, and electrical transmission lines.

Si.name: Silicon
Si.fact: It is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, after oxygen.
Si.uses: Used in computer chips and solar cells; silicon dioxide is a major glass ingredient.

P.name: Phosphorus
P.fact: Phosphorus is part of DNA, RNA, and ATP.
P.uses: Phosphate compounds are used in fertilizers; red phosphorus is used on safety-match striking surfaces.

S.name: Sulfur
S.fact: Pure sulfur commonly forms a yellow solid.
S.uses: Used to manufacture sulfuric acid and to vulcanize rubber.

Cl.name: Chlorine
Cl.fact: Chlorine belongs to the halogen family.
Cl.uses: Used to disinfect water and to manufacture PVC plastic.

Ar.name: Argon
Ar.fact: Argon is the most abundant noble gas in Earth's atmosphere.
Ar.uses: Provides a protective atmosphere in welding and some light bulbs.

K.name: Potassium
K.fact: Its symbol comes from the Latin name kalium.
K.uses: Potassium compounds are widely used in fertilizers.

Ca.name: Calcium
Ca.fact: Calcium compounds are important components of bones and teeth.
Ca.uses: Calcium compounds are used in cement, plaster, and other construction materials.

Sc.name: Scandium
Sc.fact: It is a lightweight transition metal.
Sc.uses: Small amounts are added to aluminum alloys used in specialized sporting and aerospace equipment.

Ti.name: Titanium
Ti.fact: It combines low density with strength and corrosion resistance.
Ti.uses: Used in aircraft parts and medical implants; titanium dioxide is a white pigment.

V.name: Vanadium
V.fact: Small amounts can increase the strength of steel.
V.uses: Used in high-strength steel alloys and vanadium redox flow batteries.

Cr.name: Chromium
Cr.fact: A protective chromium oxide layer helps stainless steel resist corrosion.
Cr.uses: Used in stainless steel and corrosion-resistant metal plating.

Mn.name: Manganese
Mn.fact: It is an essential trace element for living organisms.
Mn.uses: Used in steelmaking; manganese dioxide is used in some batteries.

Fe.name: Iron
Fe.fact: Iron is the main metal in Earth's core.
Fe.uses: Used to make steel for buildings, tools, vehicles, and machinery.

Co.name: Cobalt
Co.fact: Cobalt compounds can produce an intense blue color in glass.
Co.uses: Used in some rechargeable battery cathodes and high-temperature alloys.

Ni.name: Nickel
Ni.fact: Nickel is one of the elements that is ferromagnetic at room temperature.
Ni.uses: Used in stainless steel, metal plating, and rechargeable batteries.

Cu.name: Copper
Cu.fact: Copper is an excellent conductor of electricity and heat.
Cu.uses: Used in electrical wiring, plumbing, and heat exchangers.

Zn.name: Zinc
Zn.fact: A zinc coating can protect iron even when the coating is scratched.
Zn.uses: Used to galvanize steel and to make brass with copper.

Ga.name: Gallium
Ga.fact: It melts at about 30 degrees Celsius, just above typical room temperature.
Ga.uses: Gallium compounds are used in LEDs and semiconductor devices.

Ge.name: Germanium
Ge.fact: It is a metalloid used as a semiconductor.
Ge.uses: Used in fiber-optic systems and infrared optics.

As.name: Arsenic
As.fact: Arsenic is a metalloid, and many of its compounds are toxic.
As.uses: Gallium arsenide is used in semiconductor devices and some solar cells.

Se.name: Selenium
Se.fact: Its electrical conductivity can increase when it is exposed to light.
Se.uses: Used in glassmaking and in some photovoltaic materials.

Br.name: Bromine
Br.fact: Bromine is the only nonmetal that is liquid at typical room temperature.
Br.uses: Bromine compounds are used in some flame retardants and photographic materials.

Kr.name: Krypton
Kr.fact: Its name comes from a Greek word meaning hidden.
Kr.uses: Used in specialized lamps and in some insulating window units.

Rb.name: Rubidium
Rb.fact: It is a very reactive alkali metal.
Rb.uses: Used in some atomic clocks and in atomic-physics research.

Sr.name: Strontium
Sr.fact: Strontium compounds can produce a bright red flame.
Sr.uses: Used in red fireworks and signal flares.

Y.name: Yttrium
Y.fact: It is named after Ytterby, a village in Sweden.
Y.uses: Used in phosphors, ceramics, and yttrium aluminum garnet laser materials.

Zr.name: Zirconium
Zr.fact: It resists corrosion and absorbs relatively few thermal neutrons.
Zr.uses: Zirconium alloys are used as nuclear-reactor fuel cladding.

Nb.name: Niobium
Nb.fact: Niobium can form useful superconducting alloys.
Nb.uses: Used in superconducting magnets and high-strength steels.

Mo.name: Molybdenum
Mo.fact: It has a very high melting point.
Mo.uses: Used in heat-resistant steels and alloys; molybdenum compounds are also used as catalysts.

Tc.name: Technetium
Tc.fact: It was the first element to be produced artificially, and it has no stable isotopes.
Tc.uses: The radioisotope technetium-99m is used in diagnostic medical imaging.

Ru.name: Ruthenium
Ru.fact: It is a member of the platinum-group metals.
Ru.uses: Used in catalysts and to improve the durability of some electrical contacts.

Rh.name: Rhodium
Rh.fact: Rhodium is a platinum-group metal with a highly reflective surface.
Rh.uses: Used in catalytic converters and reflective or decorative metal coatings.

Pd.name: Palladium
Pd.fact: Palladium can absorb large amounts of hydrogen.
Pd.uses: Used in catalytic converters, chemical catalysts, and electronics.

Ag.name: Silver
Ag.fact: Silver has the highest electrical conductivity of any element.
Ag.uses: Used in electrical contacts, solar cells, jewelry, and mirrors.

Cd.name: Cadmium
Cd.fact: Cadmium is toxic and often occurs with zinc ores.
Cd.uses: Used in nickel-cadmium batteries and cadmium telluride solar cells.

In.name: Indium
In.fact: Indium is a soft metal that can form transparent conductive compounds.
In.uses: Indium tin oxide is used in touchscreens and flat-panel displays.

Sn.name: Tin
Sn.fact: Tin is one of the metals used to make bronze.
Sn.uses: Used in solder and as a protective coating on steel food cans.

Sb.name: Antimony
Sb.fact: Its symbol comes from the Latin name stibium.
Sb.uses: Antimony compounds are used with flame retardants, and the metal is used in some alloys.

Te.name: Tellurium
Te.fact: It is a relatively rare metalloid.
Te.uses: Used in cadmium telluride solar cells and thermoelectric materials.

I.name: Iodine
I.fact: Iodine is needed to make thyroid hormones.
I.uses: Iodine compounds are used in iodized salt and some antiseptics.

Xe.name: Xenon
Xe.fact: Although it is a noble gas, xenon can form chemical compounds.
Xe.uses: Used in some high-intensity lamps and spacecraft ion thrusters.

Cs.name: Cesium
Cs.fact: The cesium-133 atom defines the SI second.
Cs.uses: Used in atomic clocks; cesium formate solutions are used in some drilling fluids.

Ba.name: Barium
Ba.fact: Barium compounds can produce a green flame.
Ba.uses: Insoluble barium sulfate is used as an X-ray contrast material; some barium compounds are used in fireworks.

La.name: Lanthanum
La.fact: Its name comes from a Greek word meaning to lie hidden.
La.uses: Lanthanum compounds are used in optical glass and in some rechargeable battery alloys.

Ce.name: Cerium
Ce.fact: Cerium is the most abundant rare-earth element in Earth's crust.
Ce.uses: Cerium oxide is used to polish glass and in automotive catalytic converters.

Pr.name: Praseodymium
Pr.fact: Its name refers to the green color of some of its salts.
Pr.uses: Used in some strong magnet alloys and to color glass and ceramics.

Nd.name: Neodymium
Nd.fact: Neodymium is a rare-earth element used in powerful permanent magnets.
Nd.uses: Neodymium-iron-boron magnets are used in headphones, electric motors, and wind-turbine generators.
